concept: Why do raindrops fall at a steady speed instead of getting faster and faster?
title: Skyfall Tower
tagline: Watch raindrops fall and discover why they stop accelerating

science.hiddenLaw: Terminal velocity from velocity-dependent drag: a falling drop accelerates under gravity until the upward aerodynamic drag force which grows with speed (F_d = ½ C_d ρ A v² for quadratic drag, ∝ v at low Reynolds number) exactly balances downward weight mg, so net force F_net = mg - F_d → 0 and acceleration → 0, giving steady speed v_t = sqrt(2mg/(C_d ρ A)).
science.plainStatement: Raindrops stop getting faster because the faster they fall the harder the air pushes back; when the upward push of air grows to exactly equal the downward pull of their weight, the forces cancel and they fall at a steady speed.
misconceptions: Gravity alone determines falling speed and air resistance is negligible or constant - so drops should accelerate forever at g.
Terminal velocity means gravity stops acting, runs out, or is 'used up' at steady speed.
Heavier objects have greater gravitational acceleration (confusing g with v_t) - so mass changes acceleration rather than just changing the final balanced speed where drag equals weight.

sources.title: NASA Glenn Research Center - Terminal Velocity

story.setting: You are in a glass rain tower where single drops fall past sensors. You can change the air, the drop, and the pull of gravity itself.
story.mystery: Why does a falling drop settle at a steady speed instead of accelerating forever?
story.goal: Find the hidden balance that sets each drop's final speed.

predictions.prompt: What happens if you remove all air from the tower?
options: Drops still reach same steady speed

predictions.prompt: At steady speed, what is happening to gravity?
options: Gravity still pulls, balanced by air push
Gravity runs out and becomes zero
Gravity turns off at steady speed

predictions.prompt: You double the drop's weight without changing its size. What happens?
options: Same start acceleration, higher final speed
It accelerates faster from the start

transfer.setup: A skydiver opens a parachute that triples her area but keeps her weight the same as she falls through steady air.
transfer.question: What happens to her steady falling speed after the parachute opens?
options: It becomes much slower but still steady
Gravity stops pulling once parachute opens

checks.description: With air drag present, velocity initially rises then plateaus to flat terminal velocity
Control: in vacuum with no drag (dragCoeff=0, airDensity=0) velocity never plateaus but keeps increasing
At steady fall drag equals weight so net force approaches zero and acceleration approaches zero
Larger mass with same area gives higher terminal velocity (v_t ∝ sqrt(m))
